description: We are CinderTrace, a team interested in Earth science, data visualization and web development. We’re building a fire activity calendar using MODIS and VIIRS data to help people explore historical patterns. Join us to turn satellite data into clear, useful tools.
summary:
CinderTrace is an interactive web platform that turns NASA satellite fire data into accessible visual investigations. It brings together more than five million MODIS and VIIRS observations across Sri Lanka, California, and New South Wales, alongside attributed historical reference data and NASA satellite imagery.

Users can explore fire detections on a map, filter observations by time and location, compare years, examine seasonal patterns, and investigate areas near communities, health facilities, and protected landscapes. Downloadable records, charts, and PDF evidence packs help users communicate their findings.

CinderTrace addresses the challenge of making complex Earth observation data understandable and useful. It connects individual satellite records with geographic context while explaining sensor differences, missing data, and scientific limitations.

This matters because accessible, transparent fire information can support environmental education, research, and informed planning. CinderTrace helps people investigate historical patterns and ask better questions without treating satellite detections as confirmed incidents or predictions.
details:
CinderTrace is an interactive fire observation platform that helps people explore satellite detections and historical fire patterns in Sri Lanka, California, and New South Wales. It brings complex datasets into a visual experience designed for students, researchers, environmental organizations, and decision-makers.

The platform contains more than five million satellite observations from 2000–2026. Users can explore an interactive map, filter records by location, date, satellite, confidence, and other attributes, and compare patterns across years. Calendar views and seasonal charts reveal changes over time, while satellite imagery provides additional geographic context. Users can draw an area of interest, inspect individual observations, save investigations, and export selected records, charts, and PDF reports.

CinderTrace combines native NASA FIRMS observations, accessed through Portolan’s mirror catalogue, with an attributed Fire Harmony historical reference dataset. These sources are presented separately so users can understand their different meanings and limitations. The platform also includes contextual layers such as health facilities, response facilities, settlements, and protected areas to support further investigation.

Its intended impact is to make fire data more accessible and support evidence-based environmental education, research, and planning. By reducing the effort needed to explore satellite archives, CinderTrace helps users identify patterns and develop informed questions about places and periods that deserve closer attention. It is an exploratory tool; satellite detection counts do not directly represent unique fires, burned area, or confirmed damage.

We developed the platform using TypeScript, React, and Vite, with Mapbox GL, Three.js, and GSAP for interactive mapping, three-dimensional visualizations, and animation. Python supports data preparation, reconciliation, validation, and export. The frontend uses prepared static datasets, allowing it to run without a dedicated Python server. Browser-based tools support CSV downloads, chart exports, PDF generation, saved notes, and limited offline access.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting detailed scientific records with guided visual investigations. Users can move from a regional historical overview to a specific observation, compare geographic patterns, and assemble an evidence pack containing selected data, notes, and supporting context. The optional raised map view adds a visual way to explore observation density while keeping the underlying records available for inspection.

Our team considered data provenance, differences between sensors, incomplete records, geographic precision, accessibility, performance, and reproducibility. We preserve distinctions between missing data and recorded zeros, explain the limitations of each source, and avoid presenting historical estimates as predictions. Reduced-motion support, data loaded by region and year, and downloadable evidence help make the platform practical and transparent.
